newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's health fails him again.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's health fails him again.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin has until now won all the political battles he has faced, but his struggle against ill health has become the toughest of all.
He was taken to hospital with the first signs of pneumonia on Wednesday, two months after a major heart operation and less than three weeks since he returned to the Kremlin.

Yeltsin probably fell victim to his paramount passion -- to always be on top. Doctors have been urging the 65-year-old leader to take things easy after quintuple bypass surgery on November 5 but he clearly wanted to reassert his power fast.

Looking older and physically unwell, Yeltsin had maintained a busy schedule since he ruturned to the Kremlin on December 23 but had cancelled all meetings since Monday due to a heavy cold which apparently grew worse.
His health problems are not surprising.
Few contemporary politicians have faced so many battles, taken so many risks and handled problems on such a scale, or had such a roller-coaster career.

Yeltsin, who rose as a Communist Party official, then became leader of the first legal opposition in the communist superpower, crushed the party and played a pivotal role in destroying the Soviet Union.
He launched Russia's first market reforms and, in what might be considered his gravest mistake, spilt the blood of thousands of his countrymen in the breakaway region of Chechnya.
Two mild heart attacks in 1995 put him out of action for months. But Yeltsin pulled out all the stops before the June poll to prove he had what it took for four more years in power.
He criss-crossed the vast Russian Federation, keeping to a punishing schedule and adding flourishes like swinging on a swing and dancing the twist at a pop concert.
Gone was the halting walk, the slurred speech and the puffy face which had stirred rumours that heavy drinking and a weak heart might be taking their toll on the 65-year-old leader.
But the image of the Yeltsin who climbed on a tank in August 1991 to defy a communist-led putsch in Moscow disappeared abruptly when his goal was in sight.
Renat Akchurin, the doctor conducting Yeltsin's operation, has suggested the president had another heart attack at the time but that the Kremlin, fearing election defeat, concealed it.
Yeltsin finished 13 points ahead of communist Gennady Zyuganov on July 3, and immediately paid the price for the victory with his heart.
He disappeared from the public eye and on September 5 announced he had decided to have an operation in order to be able to return to active life.
He returned to the Kremlin on December 23 but signs of pneumonia hit him on January 8.
Yeltsin, elected Russian president in 1991, hit the peak of his power, strength and popularity in August that year when he defied a hardline coup against Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.

Two years after personifying the fight for democracy on the tank outside the White House, his moral authority slipped when he sent tanks against the same parliament building to crush a bloody rebellion by parliamentary hardliners.

In late 1994 Yeltsin committed what he later acknowledged to be a huge blunder, sending troops into Chechnya to end its drive for independence. Tens of thousands of people were killed in the fighting.
After last year's two mild heart attacks he said he would have preferred to retire and play with his baby grandson than face the stress of a second term in the Kremlin.
But the threat of a communist return to power kicked him out of his lethargy, prompting a sudden burst of activity.

It was this energy and ambition that has helped Yeltsin, a construction engineer by profession, buck authority and defeat the odds since his early days as a Communist Party official in the Urals industrial city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg.
When Gorbachev brought him to Moscow in 1985, he rose quickly to become a candidate member of the Politburo, then the highest power in the land, and first secretary of the party in the capital.
His demands for faster reform lost him favour and in late 1987 he was disgraced, told by Gorbachev he would never be allowed back into politics.
But in March 1989 he was elected to parliament in the country's first multi-candidate elections, gaining a phenomenal 89 per cent of the vote in Moscow.
In July 1990, he gambled again and stalked out of the Communist Party, a move which only increased his popularity.
Eleven months later he won some 57 percent of vote in the Russian Federation to become its first executive president.
Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin was born in a peasant family on February 1, 1931. He has a wife, Naina, two daughters and four grandchildren.
